title: Do LLM-derived graph priors improve multi-agent coordination?

paper.title: Do LLM-derived graph priors improve multi-agent coordination?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is crucial for AI systems
that operate collaboratively in distributed and adversarial settings,
particularly in multi-domain operations (MDO). A central challenge
in cooperative MARL is determining how agents should coordinate:
existing approaches must either hand-specify graph topology, rely on
proximity-based heuristics, or learn structure entirely from
environment interaction; all of which are brittle, semantically
uninformed, or data-intensive. We investigate whether large language
models (LLMs) can generate useful coordination graph priors for MARL
by using minimal natural language descriptions of agent observations
to infer latent coordination patterns. These priors are integrated
into MARL algorithms via graph convolutional layers within a
graph neural network (GNN)-based pipeline, and evaluated on four
cooperative scenarios from the Multi-Agent Particle Environment
(MPE) benchmark against baselines spanning the full spectrum of
coordination modeling, from independent learners to state-of-the-art
graph-based methods. We further ablate across five compact open-source
LLMs to assess the sensitivity of prior quality to model choice.
Our results provide the first quantitative evidence that LLM-derived
graph priors can enhance coordination and adaptability in dynamic
multi-agent environments, and demonstrate that models as small as
1.5B parameters are sufficient for effective prior generation.

Nikunj Gupta Rajgopal Kannan Viktor Prasanna Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Abstract Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is crucial for AI systems that operate collaboratively in distributed and adversarial settings, particularly in multi-domain operations (MDO). A central challenge in cooperative MARL is determining how agents should coordinate: existing approaches must either hand-specify graph topology, rely on proximity-based heuristics, or learn structure entirely from environment interaction; all of which are brittle, semantically uninformed, or data-intensive. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can generate useful coordination graph priors for MARL by using minimal natural language descriptions of agent observations to infer latent coordination patterns. These priors are integrated into MARL algorithms via graph convolutional layers within a graph neural network (GNN)-based pipeline, and evaluated on four cooperative scenarios from the Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) benchmark against baselines spanning the full spectrum of coordination modeling, from independent learners to state-of-the-art graph-based methods. We further ablate across five compact open-source LLMs to assess the sensitivity of prior quality to model choice. Our results provide the first quantitative evidence that LLM-derived graph priors can enhance coordination and adaptability in dynamic multi-agent environments, and demonstrate that models as small as 1.5B parameters are sufficient for effective prior generation. keywords multi-agent reinforcement learning, large language models, graph neural networks, coordination graphs, multi-domain operations, emergent coordination, cooperative artificial intelligence † † authorinfo: Further author information: (Send correspondence to Nikunj Gupta) Nikunj Gupta: E-mail: nikunj@usc.edu 1 Introduction Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has emerged as a foundational paradigm for training collections of autonomous agents to act, communicate, and coordinate within shared, dynamic environments. Its applications span a wide and growing spectrum: autonomous vehicle fleets, UAV swarms [ 38 , 1 ] , warehouse robotics [ 57 , 16 ] , distributed sensor networks [ 24 ] , human-robot teams [ 32 ] , and safety-critical military contexts such as multi-domain operations (MDO) [ 42 , 33 , 52 ] . In all of these settings, the ability of agents to coordinate (i.e., to form coherent joint strategies despite acting on local, partial observations) is not merely desirable but essential. Yet coordination remains one of the central open challenges in MARL. Agents must implicitly or explicitly reason about the intentions and observations of their teammates, often under tight computational and communication constraints [ 3 , 27 ] . Classical approaches such as independent Q-learning [ 39 ] ignore inter-agent dependencies entirely, while fully centralized methods suffer from exponential growth in the joint action space [ 56 , 28 ] . The centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm [ 17 , 2 ] has offered a principled middle ground, yielding influential value decomposition algorithms such as VDN [ 37 ] , QMIX [ 30 ] , QTRAN [ 35 ] , and QPLEX [ 46 ] . While effective, these methods treat the agent team as an undifferentiated collective, failing to explicitly model which agents should attend to which others. Graph-based MARL addresses this by encoding agent relationships as edges in a coordination graph, using GNNs [ 43 ] to propagate information along these edges and ground value factorization in explicit relational structure [ 4 , 18 , 47 , 15 , 53 , 6 , 9 ] . However, existing approaches must either hand-specify the graph topology, rely on proximity-based heuristics, or learn structure entirely from environment interaction, all of which are brittle, semantically uninformed, or data-intensive. This raises a natural question: can a richer, semantic source of prior knowledge be leveraged to initialize coordination graphs before learning begins? Large language models (LLMs) have simultaneously undergone a remarkable rise as general-purpose reasoning engines. Both large proprietary models and increasingly capable open-source alternatives have demonstrated strong performance in chain-of-thought reasoning [ 48 ] , common-sense inference, strategic planning [ 54 ] , and zero-shot policy generation for sequential decision-making tasks [ 14 , 44 ] . These capabilities are particularly relevant to multi-agent coordination for several reasons. First, LLMs encode vast prior knowledge about teamwork, roles, and strategy, distilled from human text spanning game theory, military doctrine, organizational behavior [ 25 ] , and collaborative problem-solving. Second, their strong natural language understanding enables them to interpret semantically rich descriptions of agent observations, such as unit types, relative positions, health states, and task objectives, and infer meaningful relational structure from them, a task that purely data-driven methods struggle with under limited experience [ 36 ] . Third, LLMs can perform this inference in a zero-shot fashion, requiring no environment-specific training or labeled coordination data [ 14 ] . Together, these properties suggest that LLMs may be uniquely well-positioned to serve not as direct policy executors [ 34 ] , but as structural prior generators or sources of high-level coordination knowledge that can be injected into a downstream learning system to guide and accelerate policy optimization. Figure 1: MARL applications and the coordination challenge. Agents across domains must coordinate under partial observability. We propose LLM-derived graph priors as a semantic, data-efficient alternative to heuristic or learned coordination graphs. In this paper, we investigate precisely this hypothesis. Specifically, we study whether LLMs can generate useful coordination graph priors for GNN-based MARL, and whether doing so leads to measurable improvements in fully cooperative task performance. Given minimal natural language descriptions of each agent’s local observation, we prompt an LLM to infer which agents are likely to benefit from coordinating with one another. The LLM’s output is parsed into a weighted adjacency matrix, which serves as a graph prior over the agent coordination topology. This prior is consumed by a graph neural network (GNN) [ 43 ] that aggregates agent observations and produces enriched feature representations, which in turn feed into a standard MARL policy optimization pipeline under the CTDE paradigm. We evaluate this framework on four cooperative scenarios from the Multi-Agent Particle Environment (MPE) [ 22 , 26 ] , comparing against baselines spanning the full spectrum of coordination modeling and ablating across five compact open-source LLMs to assess prior quality sensitivity to model choice. The contributions of this paper are as follows: • LLM-driven coordination graph prior generation. We propose a method for eliciting structured coordination graph priors from LLMs via natural language prompting of agent observations, requiring no task-specific fine-tuning and no ground-truth graph supervision, making it broadly applicable across cooperative MARL settings. • Empirical evaluation on MPE. We demonstrate that LLM-derived graph priors improve policy performance across four cooperative MPE environments, providing systematic comparisons against baselines spanning four categories of coordination modeling, from independent learning to state-of-the-art soft-edge graph methods [ 4 , 18 , 9 , 10 ] . • LLM sensitivity and deployability analysis. We ablate across five compact open-source models (0.5B–3B parameters) spanning three model families, demonstrating that models as small as 1.5B parameters are sufficient for effective coordination graph prior generation, and providing practical guidance for resource-constrained multi-agent deployment. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work in MARL, GNN-based coordination, and LLMs for decision-making. Section 3 describes our proposed framework. Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results on MPE. Section 5 discusses broader implications, limitations, and future directions. Section 6 concludes. 2 Background and Related Works 2.1 Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies how a team of agents can learn decentralized decision-making policies that maximize a shared objective through interaction with a common environment. This setting is commonly formalized as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) [ 3 , 27 ] , defined by the tuple ℳ = ⟨ ℐ , 𝒮 , { 𝒜 i } i ∈ ℐ , 𝒯 , ℛ , { 𝒪 i } i ∈ ℐ , 𝒪 , γ , ρ 0 ⟩ , \mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{I},\mathcal{S},\{\mathcal{A}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{R},\{\mathcal{O}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}},\mathcal{O},\gamma,\rho_{0}\rangle, (1) where ℐ = { 1 , … , n } \mathcal{I}=\{1,\dots,n\} is the set of agents, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is the global state space, 𝒜 i \mathcal{A}_{i} is the local action space of agent i i (with joint action space 𝒜 = ∏ i ∈ ℐ 𝒜 i \mathcal{A}=\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mathcal{A}_{i} ), 𝒯 ⁡ ( s ′ ∣ s , 𝐚 ) \mathcal{T}(s^{\prime}\mid s,\mathbf{a}) is the transition function, ℛ ⁡ ( s , 𝐚 ) \mathcal{R}(s,\mathbf{a}) is a shared reward function, and γ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \gamma\in(0,1) is the discount factor. Each agent receives a local observation o i ∈ 𝒪 i o_{i}\in\mathcal{O}_{i} , with joint observation space 𝒪 = ∏ i ∈ ℐ 𝒪 i \mathcal{O}=\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mathcal{O}_{i} , and the environment is initialized from ρ 0 \rho_{0} . At execution time, agent i i selects actions using only its local action–observation history, which makes coordination under partial observability the central challenge in cooperative MARL. One of the dominant frameworks for learning in Dec-POMDPs is centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) [ 17 , 2 ] . Under CTDE, global information (e.g., state or joint observations) may be used during training to stabilize learning, while each agent deploys a decentralized policy that conditions only on local information. Value decomposition is a prominent CTDE family: methods such as VDN [ 37 ] , QMIX [ 30 ] , Weighted QMIX [ 29 ] , QTRAN [ 35 ] , and QPLEX [ 46 ] factorize a centralized Q tot Q_{\mathrm{tot}} into per-agent utilities under structural constraints that permit tractable decentralized action selection. Complementary actor-critic extensions under CTDE, including MADDPG [ 22 ] and MAPPO [ 55 ] , extend this paradigm to policy gradient methods, enabling stable training with continuous action spaces and richer policy representations. More recent work has explored sequence modeling perspectives on MARL [ 49 ] , conditional policy factorization [ 45 ] , correlated policy structures [ 19 ] and uncertainty-aware action modeling [ 11 ] to further improve the expressiveness of joint value functions within the CTDE framework. Beyond algorithmic design, orthogonal lines of work have addressed the computational scalability of MARL training on modern multi-core and multi-GPU hardware [ 51 , 50 ] , reflecting the growing practical demands of deploying cooperative MARL at scale.
